slides.title: Direct Sign-In boundary
slides.subtitle: Hand authorization to the user's browser, without the model seeing OAuth
slides.notes: Direct Sign-In upgrades a signed-out Session to a signed-in one through the company's own sign-in page. This example covers the first half: everything up to the moment the user's browser opens that page.

slides.title: Why a boundary
slides.statement: The model may **explain** why sign-in is needed. The **host** builds the request.
slides.notes: The agent can tell the user that it needs access to their orders. But the OAuth request, its state and its secrets are built by host code, and the company's page opens in a trusted browser, never inside the conversation.

slides.title: Who takes part

columns.heading: Agent and model
columns.content: Asks for `orders:read` on the existing Session, then waits.

columns.heading: PAP host
columns.content: Generates state and the PKCE verifier, stores them in **Reactor**, opens the browser.

columns.heading: Browser and company
columns.content: The user signs in on the **company's** page and sees the exact scopes.

slides.notes: The model asks for a scope on a Session that already exists. The host does the OAuth work and keeps the pending request in a Reactor state store. The user's trusted browser talks to the company's authorization server.

slides.title: Up to the browser

items.title: Store
items.detail: Pending request by hashed state, with expiry

items.title: Open
items.detail: The authorization URL, in the trusted browser

slides.notes: The host makes a random state and a PKCE verifier, derives the S256 challenge, and stores the pending request under a hash of the state, with an expiry. Then it hands the authorization URL to the browser.

slides.title: The whole handoff
slides.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant M as Model
  participant H as PAP host
  participant B as Browser
  participant C as Company
  M->>H: Request orders:read
  H->>B: Open authorization URL
  B->>C: Sign-in page
  C-->>B: Authenticate, ask for scopes
  H-->>M: Waiting for user, scopes, expiry
slides.notes: Here is the handoff at once. The model asks, the host opens the company's page in the browser, the company authenticates the user and asks for the scopes, and the model is told only that it is waiting for the user.

slides.title: What the example proves
items: State and verifier come from secure randomness
Only the **S256 challenge** reaches the authorization endpoint
The authorization URL is a secret: only the browser handoff sees it
Pending state expires, and can later be consumed atomically
The company owns the sign-in UI: no password reaches the agent
slides.notes: The URL counts as a secret because it carries the state and the user's intent, so only the browser handoff capability ever receives it. And because the company owns the sign-in page, the agent never sees a password.

slides.title: What stays where
slides.notes: The model gets a status it can explain to the user: waiting, for which scopes, until when. Everything an attacker could use stays with the host.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The example stops at the browser boundary. The Direct Sign-In lifecycle example continues from the callback
slides.notes: This example ends deliberately at the browser. The complete Direct Sign-In lifecycle example picks up at the callback, with its validation and the token exchange.
